questions.stem: Which is the only reliable mitigation for SQL injection?
choices: Run as a non-root DB user
questions.explanation: Placeholders separate code from data. Escape lists are bypassable; least-privilege is defense in depth but doesn't prevent the injection.

questions.stem: Stored XSS happens when:
choices: An attacker tricks a user into clicking a malicious URL whose query parameter is reflected unescaped
Malicious JS is saved to the database and rendered to subsequent viewers
questions.explanation: Stored XSS persists in storage and victimises every later viewer. Reflected XSS lives in the URL of a single request.

questions.stem: Which Content-Security-Policy directive most effectively limits XSS impact?
questions.explanation: Restricting script-src to 'self' blocks inline scripts and external loads, neutralising most XSS payloads.

questions.stem: GET /api/orders/43 returns order 43 even when the requester owns only order 42. This is:
questions.explanation: The URL exposes the object, and the server doesn't check whether the caller may access it.

questions.stem: Why is SHA-256(password) NOT a safe password storage scheme?
choices: It is too fast — GPUs can compute billions per second, enabling offline brute-force; use bcrypt/argon2 with a work factor
questions.explanation: Password hashes must be slow on purpose. Bcrypt/argon2/scrypt include a tunable cost and salt.

questions.stem: Which cookie attributes give the strongest session protection?
questions.explanation: HttpOnly blocks JS access (XSS), Secure forces HTTPS, SameSite blocks most CSRF.

questions.stem: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) tells the browser to:
choices: Always use HTTPS to this host for the lifetime of the header
questions.explanation: HSTS prevents SSL stripping by refusing to talk HTTP to the host (and subdomains, if specified) until max-age expires.

questions.stem: An attacker uses an internal admin endpoint by making the server fetch http://169.254.169.254/. This is:
questions.explanation: SSRF: the server is tricked into fetching a URL on the attacker's behalf, often to reach private cloud metadata or internal services.

questions.stem: Which is correct about CSRF in 2026 browsers when using cookies?
choices: SameSite=Lax (modern default) blocks most CSRF on state-changing methods; tokens add defense in depth
questions.explanation: Modern browsers default cookies to Lax. Belt-and-braces apps still ship CSRF tokens for sensitive actions.

questions.stem: Which is the right header to prevent MIME sniffing?
questions.explanation: nosniff stops browsers from second-guessing the Content-Type and rendering text/plain as script, etc.

questions.stem: Which prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe (clickjacking)?
questions.explanation: frame-ancestors is the modern CSP directive. X-Frame-Options is the legacy header.

questions.stem: Why is `eval(userInput)` dangerous beyond XSS?
choices: It executes arbitrary code with full app privileges — direct remote code execution if the input is attacker-controlled
questions.explanation: Eval turns strings into running code. Avoid it entirely; if you think you need it you almost certainly don't.

questions.stem: Best mitigation for brute-force login attempts?
choices: Rate-limiting + account lockout + MFA, plus slow password hashing on the server
questions.explanation: Defense in depth: limit attempts, slow each one, require a second factor. Forced rotation is now discouraged (NIST 800-63B).

questions.stem: Which is most likely an XSS sink?
questions.explanation: innerHTML parses strings as HTML. Attribute event handlers in injected markup will run.

questions.stem: An app uses HTTPS but loads jQuery over HTTP. Result:
choices: Mixed content warning; the script load is blocked by modern browsers and the page is effectively compromisable in transit
questions.explanation: Mixed-content scripts are blocked; even if they loaded, a network attacker could swap the JS for malicious code.

questions.stem: Which is true about JWT and revocation?
choices: Stateless JWTs are valid until expiration; revocation requires a server-side blocklist or short-lived tokens with rotated refresh
questions.explanation: JWT's stateless property cuts both ways. Practical setups pair short access TTLs with refresh tokens to enable quick revocation.

questions.stem: OWASP A01 'Broken Access Control' includes:
choices: Missing/incorrect authorisation checks, IDOR, privilege escalation
questions.explanation: A01 covers all the ways authorisation fails. It has been the top category for several years.

questions.stem: Why use bcrypt's cost parameter (e.g. 12)?
choices: It scales the work per hash to keep brute-force expensive as hardware speeds up
questions.explanation: Cost = log2 rounds. Raise it as hardware improves so verifying a password stays slow enough to deter offline attacks.

questions.stem: Why are detailed error messages a security risk?
choices: Stack traces, SQL errors, or framework hints help attackers fingerprint the stack and craft targeted exploits
questions.explanation: Log details server-side, return generic messages to clients. Especially never echo SQL errors.

questions.stem: Which is true about CORS?
choices: CORS protects the server from malicious requests
CORS is a browser feature relaxing same-origin policy; servers must opt in. It does not protect the server from non-browser clients
questions.explanation: CORS keeps the browser from letting attacker JS read cross-origin responses. The server still needs its own auth/CSRF defenses.

questions.stem: Best fix for IDOR?
choices: Authorise every object access against the authenticated user's permissions, regardless of URL guessability
questions.explanation: Security through obscurity (unguessable IDs) is not enough. The server must enforce ownership on every access.

questions.stem: What does `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=()` do?
choices: Tells the browser not to grant the page (or its iframes) access to the camera/microphone APIs
questions.explanation: Permissions-Policy denies specified powerful features. Useful to scope third-party iframes.

questions.stem: What is the principle of least privilege?
choices: Give every component the minimum privileges it needs to function
questions.explanation: Limit blast radius: app DB users shouldn't own DDL; build agents shouldn't read prod data; etc.

questions.stem:
Reviewing this code: `res.send('

Hi ' + req.query.name + '

')`. The vulnerability is:
choices: Reflected XSS — query parameter rendered as HTML without escaping
questions.explanation: `?name=<script>...</script>` runs in the victim's browser. Escape or use a templating engine that auto-escapes.

questions.stem: Which is true about session fixation?
choices: The attacker steals the cookie via XSS
The attacker sets the victim's session id (e.g. via URL) before login; after login, the attacker now shares the authenticated session
It is the same as CSRF
questions.explanation: Mitigate by regenerating the session id after authentication (req.session.regenerate()).
